subtype: Approach: starting with the junior's actual goal [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday evening. Karthik came to the library corner today, the second-year I promised to mentor. I was ready to give the speech I once got: do competitive coding, do the hard problems, join every club. Then I stopped and asked, "What do you want out of this year?" Karthik said, "An internship, any internship, next summer." That changed everything. Competitive coding is not what I did for my own internship. I got it by building two small projects and putting them on a page. So I drew a simple sketch for Karthik: two projects, one clean resume, a few applications by January. It felt odd advising something different from my own story, but it made sense. Jasleen

qa.q: What does Karthik want out of this year?
qa.a: Karthik wants an internship, any internship, for next summer.

qa.q: What did Jasleen realise after hearing Karthik's goal?
qa.a: Jasleen realised that the old speech about competitive coding did not fit Karthik's aim, and that the advice needed to match it. It felt odd but sensible.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do to check that the plan works, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen could ask Karthik to review the plan in a month, because a real target like applications by January can be measured.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when the mentor asks what Karthik wants?
qa.a: Karthik probably feels listened to and clearer about the year ahead, since the advice now fits the goal.

grounding: A final-year student asks a junior what they want and tailors advice to that goal instead of repeating their own path.

subtype: Approach: breaking learning into small steps [Action]
passage:
Subject: Your plan for the next four weeks

Hi Tarun,

You said "learn programming" and that felt huge, so let's cut it up. Each week has three parts: one new concept, one exercise on it, and one small program that uses it. Week one is variables and loops. The exercise is on the sheet I attached. The program is a tiny quiz that asks you three questions and counts the score.

Send me what you have on Saturday and we'll go through it together, even if it's rough. Please don't skip a week to catch up later, just do a smaller version.

You can do this. 👍

Bhavna

qa.q: What is the small program for week one?
qa.a: The program for week one is a tiny quiz that asks three questions and counts the score.

qa.q: What is Bhavna worried about when saying not to skip a week?
qa.a: Bhavna worries that a skipped week gets harder to catch up on, so a smaller version is better than none.

qa.q: What other approach could help if Tarun finds the weekly plan too slow?
qa.a: Tarun could add an optional extra exercise, because the plan can grow while the small steps stay safe. 👍

qa.q: How might Tarun see the message compared with being told to learn programming?
qa.a: Tarun probably feels the task is now manageable, since it has clear steps and a Saturday review instead of one large aim.

grounding: A mentor turns learn programming into a weekly plan of one concept, one exercise and one small program, reviewed every Saturday.

subtype: Approach: giving the answer straight away [Pitfall]
passage: Sabina poured tea for Maria and said, "Let me tell you about my worst mentoring. When Rishi joined the team as a junior, I wanted to be the helpful senior. Every time Rishi came with a bug, I opened the code and fixed it, right there. It felt kind. Six months later Rishi couldn't find a missing bracket alone. Once I was on leave for a week, and the whole project stopped. Rishi sat in the corner, embarrassed, and said, 'I don't know how to begin without you.' I had built a helper, not a learner." She looked at Maria. "Being useful and being helpful are different things. I had confused them, and Rishi paid for it."

qa.q: How many months passed before Rishi could not find a missing bracket alone?
qa.a: Six months passed before Rishi could not find a missing bracket alone.

qa.q: What did Rishi feel when the project stopped during Sabina's leave?
qa.a: Rishi felt embarrassed and lost, and said not knowing how to begin without Sabina.

qa.q: What could Sabina have done instead of fixing every bug, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could have asked Rishi what had been tried and given a hint only after an attempt, because that builds the skill to work alone.

qa.q: How might Rishi have seen Sabina's constant fixing at the start?
qa.a: Rishi probably welcomed it as kindness at first, though it slowly took away the chance to learn.

grounding: An elder recalls solving every problem for a junior, who became dependent and could not manage alone.

passage: In the computer lab of a college in Valencia, Pablo stared at a red error on the screen and turned to the mentor, Mateo. "It doesn't work. Can you fix it?" Mateo pulled up a chair but kept both hands off the keyboard. "What have you tried so far?" Pablo listed two changes. "And what does the message say?" Pablo read it aloud, slowly, and frowned. "It says the variable isn't defined." "Where do you define it?" A pause. Pablo scrolled up, found the line, and laughed. The variable was set after it was used. Mateo only nodded. Later, when Pablo got stuck on a harder loop, Mateo offered a single hint, and the rest came from Pablo.

qa.q: What did the error message say?
qa.a: The error message said the variable isn't defined.

qa.q: What did Pablo feel when finding the line that caused the error?
qa.a: Pablo laughed, with a mix of relief and amusement at having found the mistake alone.

qa.q: What could Mateo do if Pablo gets stuck again with no ideas to try?
qa.a: Mateo could suggest one small thing to test, since a hint after an attempt is better than the full answer. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pablo see the questions compared with being handed the fix?
qa.a: Pablo may feel more capable, because the answer came from Pablo's own reading and searching.

grounding: A mentor asks a stuck junior what has been tried and what the error says, and gives a hint only after an attempt.

subtype: Approach: analogy to own early struggles [Thinking]
passage: On the rooftop of the boys' hostel in the small town, Yamini sat with Darshan after the first coding test results. Darshan had scored badly and looked at the floor. "Everyone else understands this. I am not made for it." Yamini was quiet, then said, "My first coding round I failed. I could not even write the loop. I told nobody for a week. I thought everyone in the room knew what I did not." Darshan looked up. "You did?" "I did. Then I sat with a senior who showed me how to trace one line at a time. It was slow, and then it wasn't." Darshan let out a long breath. The fear had not vanished, but it felt shared now.

qa.q: What did Yamini fail in the first coding round?
qa.a: Yamini could not even write the loop in the first coding round.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the low test score?
qa.a: Darshan felt ashamed and doubtful, and believed everyone else understood the work while Darshan was not made for it.

qa.q: What could Darshan try next, and why?
qa.a: Darshan could trace a program one line at a time with a senior, because Yamini found that slow method worked in the end.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about telling the story of failing?
qa.a: Yamini probably felt a little exposed but hopeful that it would help, since sharing it made the fear seem common.

grounding: A mentor recalls failing a first coding round and tells the junior honestly to show that the fear is common and can be worked through.

subtype: Approach: pushing own path as the only path [Pitfall]
passage:
Pankaj: ok so the plan. do contest problems every day. 3 a day minimum
Mahima: I was thinking of doing the app design project this month?
Pankaj: design is not a real path. contests are what companies notice
Mahima: I like the design side though
Pankaj: it's how I got in. there is no other way
Mahima: maybe I could try both?
Pankaj: no. half effort = no result. do the problems first
Mahima: ok
Pankaj: send me your solutions tonight
Mahima: I'll try
(4 days later)
Pankaj: you haven't sent anything
Mahima: sorry, been busy. I don't think I'll do the weekly calls anymore. thanks anyway

qa.q: How many contest problems a day did Pankaj tell Mahima to do?
qa.a: Pankaj told Mahima to do three contest problems a day at minimum.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling about the plan Pankaj pushed?
qa.a: Mahima felt unheard, since Mahima liked design and was told it was not a real path, and lost interest in the calls.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do to win Mahima back, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could ask what Mahima enjoys about design and help plan from there, because advice fits when it starts from the junior's interest.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have seen the plan when giving it?
qa.a: Pankaj probably believed it was helpful, since it was the route that had worked for Pankaj, but did not see that Mahima's interest was different.

grounding: A mentor insists their own competitive-coding route is the only path though the junior enjoys design, and the junior loses interest.

subtype: Approach: agreeing on a simple check-in routine [Action]
passage: In the corner of the department library, Mahima and Jasleen sat with two cups of tea and a laptop. The first burst of energy after the introduction had been high, and Mahima knew from experience that such things fade by the third week. "Let's fix something small," Mahima said. "A ten-minute call every Sunday at eight." Jasleen agreed at once. Together they opened a shared notes file and made three headings: goals, next steps, doubts. Jasleen typed the first goal, a small web page by month end. Mahima added a first doubt of their own, about time. They saved the file, set the Sunday reminder on both phones, and the librarian tapped a watch, closing time. It was a very simple plan.

qa.q: At what time on Sunday did they fix the call?
qa.a: They fixed the call for a ten-minute chat every Sunday at eight.

qa.q: Why did Mahima want to fix a routine so soon?
qa.a: Mahima worried from experience that early enthusiasm fades by the third week, and wanted something small that would last.

qa.q: What could they try if a Sunday call is missed, and why?
qa.a: They could swap it for a short written update in the notes file, since the routine survives when the format bends. 🙂

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the shared notes file?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels supported and clear about next steps, since goals and doubts are written where both can see them.

grounding: A mentor and junior agree a short Sunday call and a shared notes file with goals, next steps and doubts.

passage: At the bus stand of a small town, Chetan waited with Parveen for the evening bus. The junior had printed a resume at the cyber café and held it out proudly. Chetan read it carefully. "The layout is neat and you have listed your skills well. But it tells me what you studied, not what you did. Where are the results?" Parveen's face fell a little. Chetan took a pen, crossed out a vague line, and wrote a sample: "Built a small billing page used by two local shops." "Like that. Something you achieved." Parveen read it twice and smiled. "I do have things like that." The bus came, and Parveen folded the paper carefully.

qa.q: Where did Parveen print the resume?
qa.a: Parveen printed the resume at the cyber café.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel when Chetan asked where the results were?
qa.a: Parveen's face fell a little, which suggests disappointment, but then Parveen smiled on seeing the sample.

qa.q: What could Chetan do next to help Parveen, and why?
qa.a: Chetan could ask Parveen to rewrite two more lines in the same style, because practising the change is easier than being told.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Chetan's mix of praise and correction?
qa.a: Parveen may find it trustworthy and helpful, since real strengths were named before the weak part.

grounding: A mentor tells the junior a resume lacks results, shows one improved example and praises real strengths, without flattery or harshness.

subtype: Approach: recognising own limits and referring on [Revision]
passage:

Madhav: honestly I don't know robotics at all
Alka: oh. I thought you knew everything in tech

Madhav: there's a senior, Mihir, in the mechatronics group. I'll message him now and introduce you

qa.q: Which field did Alka ask Madhav about?

qa.q: Why did Madhav say the honest answer instead of guessing?
qa.a: Madhav worried that guessing about motors and control might send Alka the wrong way, so it was better to admit the limit.

grounding: When a junior asks about a field the mentor does not know, the mentor says so and introduces a senior from that field.

subtype: Approach: adjusting the approach after low progress [Revision]
passage: Sunday night. Vasudha missed three weekly tasks in a row. I was about to feel irritated, then decided to ask instead. Over tea Vasudha said quietly, "The plan clashes with my exams. I'm sorry, I didn't know how to say it." I felt a little ashamed, because I had made the plan in September and never looked at the exam calendar. So we cut it down: for the next two weeks, one small exercise instead of three, and the Saturday review moves to fifteen minutes. We'll return to the full plan after exams. Vasudha looked lighter. Lesson for me: low progress can be a sign that my plan is wrong, not that the junior is lazy. Vaibhav

qa.q: How many weekly tasks had Vasudha missed in a row?
qa.a: Vasudha had missed three weekly tasks in a row.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on learning the reason for the missed tasks?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt a little ashamed, because the plan had been made without checking the exam calendar.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do after the two lighter weeks, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could ask Vasudha to help set the next plan, since shared planning shows constraints earlier.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see the mentor asking why instead of scolding?
qa.a: Vasudha probably feels relieved and safer speaking up, since the reason was heard and the plan was lightened.

grounding: A mentor sees the junior missing tasks, asks why, learns the plan clashes with exams and lightens it for two weeks.
